questions.question: Define non-conventional energy sources, explain the two properties that rule the family, and present the evidence that South Africa's endowment is exceptional, including the mechanism through which plants get built.
questions.expected_answer: Non-conventional sources are the challengers to the fossil-and-nuclear order — solar and wind above all, plus biomass and biogas, geothermal, wave and tidal power and small-scale hydro. Most are renewable, their flows replenishing naturally, though the terms are cousins rather than twins — a feedlot biogas digester is non-conventional and renewable but tiny. Two properties rule everything: the fuel costs nothing — sunshine and wind arrive daily without mining, railing or importing, so nearly all the cost sits in the catching machine — and the supply is intermittent — the sun sets and the wind takes unscheduled leave, so non-conventional power must be paired with storage, backup or a designed mix. The endowment: most of the interior receives more than two thousand five hundred sunshine hours a year, the Northern Cape's daily radiation ranks with the strongest reliably measured anywhere, and two oceans drive dependable winds onto the Eastern Cape, Western Cape and west coast; Germany built world solar leadership on roughly half our sunshine, proving the resource was never South Africa's constraint. Delivery happens through REIPPPP, the auction programme in which private developers bid to build wind and solar plants and sell power on long-term contracts — since 2011 it has mobilised hundreds of billions of rand, delivered over a hundred plants, and driven prices below new coal per unit.

questions.question: Compare photovoltaic and concentrated solar power as technologies, and describe how a wind turbine generates electricity, using named South African and world examples for both solar and wind.
questions.expected_answer: PV panels convert light directly into electricity in semiconductor cells — no moving parts, no water, output tracking daylight and peaking at noon; CSP instead uses fields of sun-tracking mirrors to concentrate heat onto a receiver where molten salt reaches several hundred degrees, raising steam for a conventional turbine — and its trump card is storage, since insulated salt tanks stay hot for hours and let the plant generate after sunset. South African solar examples cluster in the Northern Cape: PV farms like Jasper and Droogfontein near Kimberley and De Aar, and CSP at Kathu Solar Park with about four and a half hours of storage, Bokpoort near Groblershoop with roughly nine, and Ilanga outside Upington; rooftop PV boomed during load-shedding and the solar water heater remains the cheapest solar of all. World examples: China dominates panel manufacture and installed capacity, Germany proved policy beats cloud, and Spain's Andalusian plants pioneered molten-salt storage. A wind turbine converts kinetic energy to electricity: moving air turns aerodynamic blades, the blades a shaft, the shaft a generator — no heat, steam or water — and because power grows with swept area and the cube of wind speed, doubling the wind gives eight times the power, so towers exceed a hundred metres. South African farms: Gibson Bay, Kouga and Amakhala Emoyeni in the Eastern Cape, Gouda in the Western Cape, Sere on the west coast and Loeriesfontein in the Northern Cape. World: Denmark draws about half its electricity from wind and exports the technology, China hosts the largest fleet, and the North Sea nations build offshore where winds are strongest.

questions.question: Evaluate the future of non-conventional energy in South Africa: its economic and environmental effects in both columns, and the three obstacles that will determine the pace of the transition.
questions.expected_answer: Economic positives: new wind and solar are the cheapest new electricity in the country, restraining future tariffs; REIPPPP has drawn hundreds of billions of rand of private investment; construction and maintenance work reaches rural districts the industrial economy bypassed, with the Northern Cape hosting plant worth billions; community trusts convert revenue into local development; and localisation offers a green manufacturing ladder. Economic negatives: coal supports around ninety thousand concentrated mining jobs in Mpumalanga towns with few alternatives, while finished renewable plants employ small permanent crews, usually elsewhere — the transition shifts work across provinces and skills, which is why a just transition of retraining, pensions and replacement industry, partly financed by international climate packages, is essential. Environmental effects: against the coal baseline the gains are overwhelming — no carbon dioxide, no sulphur dioxide or smog, and near-zero water use, decisive in a dry country — though honest accounting lists land footprints, bird and bat mortality without careful siting, and the material demands of manufacturing and disposing of panels, blades and batteries. The three obstacles: the grid, because the best resources sit in the Northern and Eastern Cape far from Gauteng's demand and the transmission corridors are saturated, making new lines the binding constraint; intermittency, managed by the mix — night-blowing coastal wind, CSP salt and batteries, pumped storage and peaking gas or hydro; and policy certainty, since investment flows when auction rounds run on schedule. Conclusion: the resource is world-class, so the future turns on delivery — wires, storage, policy and justice — and the only real argument is speed.
